Stated Claim / Post Context:
Gov. JB Pritzker runs for rare third term on his record but few new plans for Illinois

Pritzker, a possible 2028 presidential contender, is running on unfinished business rather than bold proposals. He’s left tax overhauls to lawmakers and pushed blame for high property taxes onto local governments as state budget pressures m…

Actual Article Body:

eNewspaper

Trending:

Celebrating his 2022 election victory over southern Illinois lawmaker Darren Bailey and looking ahead to another four years in Springfield, Gov. JB Pritzker claimed the mantle of the “happy warrior.”

The billionaire Democrat has spent much of the past two years emphasizing the “warrior” half of that moniker, long associated with onetime presidential nominee, former Vice President Hubert Humphrey. During the second half of his second term, Pritzker periodically has grabbed the national spotlight as one of the most vocal critics of Republican President Donald Trump’s reprise.

But as early voting opened across all 50 Chicago wards 15 days before this Election Day on Nov. 3, Pritzker reminded a gathering of faith leaders of his “happy” side, the optimistic approach he has taken to addressing the problems facing the state and country.

“We’ve gotten into a bad habit — a bad habit, all of y’all — of spending so much time fretting about what could go wrong that we’ve forgotten to imagine what could go right,” Pritzker told the ecumenical assembly at Evening Star Missionary Baptist Church in the South Side’s Oakland neighborhood. “I’m running for reelection because I believe that things can go right.

“If you work a full-time job, you ought to make enough money with that one job to put food on your table, to see a doctor when you’re sick, to live in a dignified home, to save for retirement, and to take a vacation every once in a while. We can and we ought to make that happen. That work lies ahead.”

Missing from Pritzker’s almost 20-minute address that day — and from his campaign for a rare third term generally — was a big-picture, state-level agenda for tackling affordability, a focal point of races up and down the ballot this year, or many of the other vexing problems facing Illinois.

In an interview at his Loop campaign headquarters that afternoon, after marching with clergy members to an early voting site, Pritzker laid out a concise program he believes Democrats in Washington should pursue if the party takes control of Congress after Tuesday’s midterms: “raising the (federal) minimum wage from $7.25 (per hour) to pick your number, giving people universal paid leave, making sure that we are delivering … an actual universal healthcare program.”

When it came to what he would do as the first Democrat elected to three terms as Illinois governor, however, Pritzker — widely considered a potential contender for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination — was less precise and less succinct.

“A lot of times people think, ‘Oh, it’s got to be, here’s a new education thing; here’s a new healthcare thing,’ right?” Pritzker said. “When, in reality, many of the long-term affordability challenges that people face are the very ones that we’re working very hard underneath, and it’s one of the reasons I’m running for reelection. Some of those things have been taking years to effectuate.”

The lack of a comprehensive third-term agenda reflects Pritzker’s ability to run on a record of accomplishments, including a minimum wage increase in his first term and a statewide paid leave law in his second. It also reflects his reluctance to make campaign promises that could be hard to keep, even with likely large Democratic majorities in the legislature.

The strategy is not dissimilar to the one Pritzker deployed en route to a nearly 13-percentage-point victory four years ago. It’s perhaps even safer this year given Bailey’s lackluster campaign fundraising and Trump’s deep unpopularity, which is expected to drag down Republican candidates in Illinois and across the country.

Incumbents who “feel like they have a strong record” and “fit in comfortably with the bigger political narrative that’s going on that cycle” can be less inclined to make big, bold policy proposals when running for another term, said Tabitha Bonilla, a Northwestern University political scientist and author of “The Importance of Campaign Promises.”

With a list of successes in Springfield and a national profile built on standing up to Trump, Pritzker fits that mold, Bonilla said.

“He can rely on his past record,” she said. “That kind of feels like a really safe track and much less risky because he’s not throwing anything new or unexpected into the mix.”

Indeed, many of the specifics Pritzker has offered amount to unfinished business from his current term rather than new proposals for the next one.

As an example of how he’d tackle affordability, the governor pointed to efforts to lower energy costs by “attracting a nuclear company to build more nuclear power in the state,” made possible by his repeal of a decades-old moratorium.

“That process takes a long time,” he said. “But it is underway, and I’ve been very much engaged in that.”

Pritzker also has said he will keep pushing his affordable housing plan, which would make it easier to build multifamily dwellings in areas now zoned for single-family homes. A cornerstone of his election-year agenda in Springfield, it stalled this spring amid pushback from local governments.

He also wants to finish a plan from early in his current term to add 20,000 seats to state-funded preschool programs over four years. After adding 11,000 seats in the first two years, the expansion has been on hold amid state budget constraints.

Bailey’s affordability agenda includes a promise to suspend the 48.3-cent-per-gallon gas tax for six months through an executive order, a legally questionable proposal given that the Illinois Constitution gives the legislature “​the exclusive power to raise revenue by law.”

Pritzker has made stabilizing the state’s chronically shaky finances, including 12 credit rating upgrades during his tenure, a central campaign theme.

But the budget constraints likely will worsen in the near term because of economic uncertainty, deepened by Trump’s tariff policies and the war in Iran, and because of federal cuts to healthcare and food assistance.

That reality could pose a risk for Pritzker’s longer-term political ambitions, said Pete Giangreco, a Democratic consultant.

“Third terms generally don’t go well,” he said. “And I think, if you’re going to run for president, you wear every mistake, every calamity, every unforeseen circumstance, you own it because you’re the governor. And I’m not sure that being an incumbent governor at a time where, despite the credit upgrades, the state’s finances are still in a pretty tricky situation, I’m not sure that’s the best way to run for president.”

Pritzker hasn’t put forward a broad plan to raise new revenue or proposed significant cuts elsewhere to cover those costs or pay for other third-term priorities.

Since voters in 2020 rejected his proposed state constitutional amendment to allow a graduated-rate income tax, Pritzker and his team have focused on a year-by-year approach to balancing the budget rather than pursuing large-scale structural changes.

Pritzker campaigned on the graduated tax in 2018 and spent $58 million of his own money trying unsuccessfully to sway voters to his side. Now he is leaving any new attempt at an income tax amendment to lawmakers.

“I spent a lot of money to try to effectuate it. We got the legislature to do what they needed to do, and then we gave it to the voters, and they chose not to. That’s fine. I understand,” Pritzker said. Under the state constitution, the governor has no formal role in the amendment process, but Pritzker’s political and financial support would be instrumental in convincing voters to approve one.

“I think there are different approaches, by the way, that might be more popular among the public, and so I’ve said to the legislature, ‘You guys know your constituents. You know what you would vote for. You know I’m here. You know what I believe, and so if you come up with something that will work, let’s move forward,’” he said.

Pritzker has similarly been hands-off on a comprehensive approach to one of the state’s most discussed and complex challenges: Property taxes that are among the highest in the nation. It’s a subject that touches on a vast range of state concerns, from election-year worries about affordability to calls for more equitable education funding to the long-running Chicago Bears stadium saga.

In 2019, his first year in office, Pritzker signed a law creating a task force to propose property tax relief, but the group disbanded without issuing official recommendations.

Since then, Pritzker has been quick to note property taxes are levied locally, shifting responsibility for lowering bills to school districts and municipalities.

Pritzker argues his administration has taken a host of steps that should make it easier for school boards and other local governments to cut taxes, including increasing state education funding by at least $300 million in all but one year he’s been in office, making it possible to collect local sales tax on online purchases, legalizing recreational cannabis, expanding video gambling at bars and restaurants and putting more state dollars into local road and building projects, among other measures.

“Have local governments alleviated enough local property taxes? No,” Pritzker said. “Some places, by the way, hard to do. Some places, easier to do.”

Some wealthy suburban school districts have continued raising property taxes annually, he said, even while sitting on large rainy day funds, a phenomenon he blamed on funding uncertainty under his predecessor, one-term Republican Gov. Bruce Rauner.

Asked for specific examples, Pritzker’s campaign shared an Illinois State Board of Education report showing almost a third of the state’s 842 school districts had enough cash on hand during the 2024-25 school year to cover expenses for 360 days or more. The board’s financial health ratings give their top reserve score to districts that can cover at least 180 days’ expenses.

Despite Illinois increasing money flowing to schools through the state’s evidence-based funding formula by $2.5 billion during Pritzker’s tenure, when factoring in such other costs as special education, transportation and construction, school districts statewide still derived 64% of their revenue from local sources, mainly property taxes, as of the 2025 budget year, according to the most recent state data available Thursday. When Pritzker took office, that figure was 66%.

Meaningfully reducing property tax bills for Illinois homeowners and businesses would require the state to take on a much larger share of the cost of elementary and secondary education, likely through the income tax or sales taxes.

For real estate tax bills to go down, “(the) money has to come from somewhere else,” said David Merriman, a University of Illinois Chicago professor who specializes in public finance.

As the defeat of Pritzker’s 2020 graduated income tax proposal showed, “Illinois, for a Democratic state, is an extremely anti-tax state,” Merriman said.

That makes proposals such as extending the sales tax to more services or taxing retirement income, both of which Pritzker has repeatedly rejected, politically unpalatable.

Bailey has proposed capping the real estate tax rate at 1% of a property’s purchase price, but that plan could blow holes in municipal and school budgets as they struggle to keep up with inflation. Such a proposal also could discourage home sales and create an “inequitable” system where owners of “similar houses would pay very different property taxes,” Merriman said.

Collin Corbett, a former Republican strategist running for governor as an independent, also has criticized Pritzker on the issue, writing in a recent social media post that “instead of solving the problem, JB Pritzker just points fingers.” Corbett’s plan, in part, calls for expanding the sales tax to services and eliminating it on some everyday essentials to boost state funding for schools and municipalities.

For some local government leaders, it has been frustrating to see Pritzker repeatedly point the finger at them on property taxes while they’ve had to lobby Springfield every year to protect their share of state income tax revenue. In his original budget proposal this year, for example, Pritzker sought to reduce the local share so the state could keep an estimated $60 million in additional revenue from rising tax collections. The Democratic-controlled legislature rejected the idea.

Local leaders’ frustrations have been compounded by Pritzker’s oft-repeated campaign message that he “eliminated the state grocery tax.” In reality, while the state Department of Revenue collects the 1% sales tax on groceries, all the revenue went to local governments.

So before the repeal Pritzker signed took effect Jan. 1, local governments faced a political Catch-22: Give up the revenue or take the heat for voting to reinstate the tax. More than half of the state’s roughly 1,300 cities and villages chose to reinstate it, according to Department of Revenue data.

Local leaders are willing to work with the state on tough problems, Illinois Municipal League CEO Brad Cole said, noting a measure approved in Pritzker’s first term that consolidated the investments of hundreds of local police and firefighter pension funds.

“The bottom line to the issue of property taxes, or anything else regarding shared revenues, (is that) the state has to be a partner with the local governments,” Cole said. “They have to be a real partner, not just saying they’re a partner.”

“At the end of the day, the bills still have to get paid,” he added, “so where’s the money going to come from? If it’s not going to come from the state, OK. But that means it has to come locally, and then the state can’t complain that the local governments are raising the money locally, which is through property tax.”

The lack of third-term specifics hasn’t kept Pritzker from winning over some unlikely supporters.

On Monday, the Illinois Retail Merchants Association, which sat out the 2018 and 2022 governor’s races and opposed Pritzker’s minimum wage increase, endorsed the governor for a third term.

“While we may not always agree, he has demonstrated a consistent willingness to listen and seek compromise where possible — valuable traits for an effective and engaged leader,” Rob Karr, the group’s president and CEO, said in a statement.

On Wednesday, Pritzker’s Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity and the retailers group proposed a package of tax incentives for independent grocery stores and pharmacies, to be considered in the current term.

Earlier this month, former Illinois House Republican leader Jim Durkin also backed the Democrat for another term. Durkin clashed with Pritzker over taxes and criminal justice issues but worked with him on a budget and capital construction plan during the governor’s first year and voted for his 2023 assault weapon ban. His endorsement was driven partly by animosity toward Trump and Bailey, who he said has “a delusional egomaniacal view of the world.”

For others, Pritzker’s focus on standing up to Trump, particularly during last year’s Operation Midway Blitz immigration crackdown, is a selling point, not a distraction from state issues.

That was the case for several veterans organizations that endorsed Pritzker earlier this month at an event at the Mid-America Carpenters Regional Council’s Near North Side headquarters.

“Last fall, after Operation Midway Blitz, Chicago didn’t feel like home,” said Army veteran Chris Gentry, West Side organizer for the progressive veterans group Common Defense. “It felt like war. Black Hawk helicopters flew low over the South Side. Masked, heavily armed men in camouflage rolled through our own neighborhoods in unmarked cars. The tamale lady that’s been selling tamales around my house for years was kidnapped.”

Gentry said he came out to support Pritzker “because I saw who stood up when it mattered in that moment.” He cited the governor’s backing of a lawsuit that blocked Trump from deploying the National Guard during the blitz, his creation of the Illinois Accountability Commission to document alleged federal misconduct, and other measures.

“This is what leadership looks like as a veteran,” Gentry said. “It’s not about who talks the toughest. It’s about who holds the line when the pressure is real, and who remembers that the oath is to the Constitution, not to the man.”

Accepting the veterans groups’ endorsements, Pritzker kept the focus on Trump while also making a relatively rare reference to his opponent.

“We’ve still got two more years of the Trump era,” Pritzker said. “It’s going to take a hell of a lot of fortitude to get through the next 27 months, and we’re not going to let Darren Bailey roll out the red carpet in Illinois to bring Trump’s failed policies to our veterans. Here in Illinois, we’ll always show up — always show up — for our patriots.”
